The figure on this page comes from one line of markdown:

```markdown
![Mean ratings by condition.](ratings.png){#fig-ratings .wrap-right width="40%"}
```

## Result

Participants rated each clip on a scale from one to five. The study
compared a control condition with a treatment condition, and the figure in
this section shows the mean rating in each one. This paragraph comes before
the figure, so it runs the full width of the text.

![Mean ratings by condition.](../images/ratings.png){#fig-ratings .wrap-right width="40%"}

@fig-ratings shows that ratings in the treatment condition were higher
than ratings in the control condition. The figure keeps its number and its
caption, and this paragraph can point to it with a `@fig-` link.

The class `.wrap-right` puts the figure on the right side of the text, and
the `width` attribute makes it 40% of the text width. The paragraphs after
the figure flow on its left. Each format draws this layout with its own
tools: CSS in HTML, wrapfig in LaTeX, wrap-it in Typst, and a frame in
Word. The text does not stay in a column of its own. After the text passes
the bottom of the figure, each line starts at the left edge of the text
and runs to the right edge, under the figure. This paragraph shows it: its
first lines sit beside the figure, and its last lines run under it. Two
columns or a table cannot give this layout, because their text stays in
its own column from top to bottom. Wrapping goes on in this way until the
next block that is not a paragraph, such as the heading below.

## Next

A heading is not a paragraph, so wrapping stops before it.
